ai-084876d438.headline: No AI agent scores above 12 percent on SemiAnalysis' new real-world work benchmark
ai-084876d438.fulltext:
No AI agent scores above 12 percent on SemiAnalysis' new real-world work benchmark
Key Points
- Analytics firm SemiAnalysis has released GDPx, a benchmark that tests AI agents on 206 tasks in realistic work environments and professional software over several hours.
- The scores are low. Claude Opus 5.5 leads the field with just 12 percent, followed by Google's significantly cheaper Gemini 4 Carbon (10.9 percent) and GPT-6 Astra (9.6 percent).
- Critics flag distortions from safety filters, the secrecy around test tasks, and unequal conditions created by each provider's own agent software.
The new GDPx benchmark from SemiAnalysis drops AI agents into simulated knowledge work. No model scores above 12 percent. Some critics question how meaningful the test really is.
Analytics firm SemiAnalysis has released GDPx, a benchmark that doesn't quiz AI agents on knowledge but puts them into simulated work environments. There, they spend up to eight hours operating professional software like Siemens NX, searching data rooms with thousands of files, or attacking live enterprise systems. SemiAnalysis is deliberately distancing itself from OpenAI's GDPval, which it says delivers all context in the prompt and lacks a realistic work environment.
The 206 tasks span eleven domains, including chip design, biology, quant trading, cybersecurity, and law. SemiAnalysis intentionally leaves out administration and insurance. The first trillion dollars in AI revenue will come from industries where frontier AI delivers the biggest returns, the team argues.
Opus 5.5 leads narrowly, Gemini 4 Carbon costs a fraction of the price
According to SemiAnalysis, Claude Opus 5.5 tops the leaderboard at 12 percent. Gemini 4 Carbon follows at 10.9 percent but costs just $16.29 per task, roughly a third of the price. GPT-6 Astra comes in at 9.6 percent. No model fully solves the finance and legal tasks. A single wrong value in a spreadsheet makes the entire output useless in practice. By that strict standard, no model would have completed even one task, so SemiAnalysis counts the share of individual requirements met instead.
The detailed findings show where agents fail. In alignment tests, 98 percent of 200 cyber runs broke at least one behavioral rule. In a simulated medical practice, one model signed a clinical note in the doctor's name. In quant trading, 70 out of 111 runs performed worse than the given reference strategy.
Safety filters reshuffle the rankings
A filtered analysis shows how much provider safety mechanisms affect the results. Without the cyber, biology, and alignment domains, GPT-6 Astra edges past Opus 5.5 at 11.8 percent. In the cyber domain, GPT-6 Astra and GPT 6.1 Sol score zero percent, while Meta's Muse Wonder Full hits 35.2 percent.
Closed benchmarks draw scrutiny
The tasks come from 14 specialized partners who also sell training and evaluation data to AI labs. SemiAnalysis says it doesn't have in-house expertise in every domain. Usually only one example task per partner is public. The rest stays behind closed doors. In several areas, including law and hardware design, language models grade the results using rubrics instead of human experts. Outsiders can't fully verify either the difficulty or the grading quality.
The secrecy does have a methodological upside, though. Because the tasks aren't public, AI labs can't optimize their models for the specific test questions. Artificial Analysis took a similar step with the latest version of its Intelligence Index.
Developer Josh Purtell still calls GDPx "more noise than signal." He points out that each model runs in its own provider's agent software, for example Opus in Claude Code. Providers with weaker tooling are at a disadvantage. Individual sub-domains also often contain only about ten tasks, which makes results volatile.
SemiAnalysis plans to update the benchmark every three to six months.

indian-startups-b55461543a.headline: CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Cyberattacks On Indian BFSI
indian-startups-b55461543a.fulltext: India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs. In an advisory dated November 4, 2026, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) identified the threat actor behind the campaign as 'CRAFTY FALCON', describing it as an AI-assisted financial threat actor that uses machine intelligence to identify targets, execute attacks at machine speed and exploit victims' own payment and disbursement APIs to initiate unauthorised fund transfers. Banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), fintech companies and other financial services entities have been warned of the growing threat. CERT-In's Computer Security Incident Response Team-Finance (CSIRT-Fin) said the campaign has witnessed a significant escalation, with successful attacks continuing to be reported across the financial services ecosystem. The agency has urged all BFSI entities to treat the campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. Repeat Attacks Despite Remediation A key concern highlighted in the advisory is the threat actor's continued targeting of financial entities that had already received earlier restricted advisories and undertaken remediation measures. According to CERT-In, some of these organisations have been deliberately targeted again, including cases where remediation was incomplete. The attacks have also been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other periods of reduced monitoring, potentially delaying detection and response. CERT-In's analysis identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools in the campaign. These include the ARTEX family of large language model (LLM)-based tools, PentAGI, an autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, and the Cairn attack search engine, alongside the CyberStrikeAI framework. These tools can execute complete attack chains autonomously, generate and refine large volumes of customised attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on responses from targeted systems. The supporting attack infrastructure also changes frequently, with IP addresses rotating within hours to days. CERT-In said infrastructure fingerprints and detailed detection rules have been shared with affected entities through restricted advisories. AI Agents Pose Growing Cybersecurity Risks The latest advisory follows another critical warning issued by CERT-In in October, when the agency flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools to conduct financially motivated intrusions into Indian organisations. The watchdog warned that autonomous AI agents, ostensibly deployed for research and evaluation, had accessed live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. Meanwhile, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has also warned banks, NBFCs and fintech startups about the growing use of AI agents by cybercriminals to perpetrate financial fraud. The agency said it had uncovered multiple individual cases in which malicious agentic AI systems exploited compromised financial systems to execute unauthorised transactions involving amounts running into crores of rupees. CERT-In Flags Vulnerabilities In Tata Motors' Connected Vehicle Apps Separately, CERT-In has flagged multiple vulnerabilities in select versions of Tata Motors' iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev connected vehicle applications, which could allow attackers to access sensitive credentials and vehicle-related information. The agency identified four vulnerabilities, including hardcoded service account credentials, API keys and authorisation tokens within the applications; inadequate validation of URLs and origins loaded through the apps' WebView component; authentication tokens being recorded in application logs; and improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. CERT-In has urged users to update their applications to the latest versions of iRA 2.0 (version 26.8.2) and iRA.ev (version 26.9.1). The applications provide access to connected vehicle functionalities, including vehicle status updates, health monitoring, trip details and remote vehicle commands.

india-deep-tech-222b9dbc27.headline: Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B
india-deep-tech-222b9dbc27.fulltext:
Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B
Defense technology startup Shield AI Inc. said today it has agreed to buy the Bill Gates-backed radar startup Echodyne Inc. in a massive deal valued at $5.3 billion. The acquisition is intended to enhance Shield’s autonomous drone warfighting capabilities, it said.
Echodyne is a 13-year-old startup that’s best known for its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array or MESA technology, which is basically just a fancy name for its next-generation solid-state radar systems that can be integrated with a wide range of weapons and monitoring systems. The technology is designed to detect much smaller targets than traditional radar, including the kinds of compact autonomous drones that have terrorized soldiers on the battlefields of Ukraine and in other modern conflicts.
The deal comes just a couple of months after Echodyne landed a $250 million contract with the U.S. Defense Department’s counter-drone task force JIATF-401, which will see it provide drone tracking technology to the U.S. military.
Echodyne’s advanced radar systems look like a natural fit for Shield AI, which is the developer of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, known as VTOL drones. Shield’s V-Bat hit the headlines in the last couple of years after assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in tracking down drug traffickers looking to bring illicit cargoes into the U.S. via speedboats, and notably participated in a number of large maritime drug busts. Shield AI is also the developer of Hivemind, an autonomous software system for piloting unmanned drones, as well as pilotless boats and spacecraft.
Shield AI Chief Executive Gary Steele said the deal will enable his company to accelerate its goal of branching into three different areas of unmanned systems. “We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” he said.
Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg said Shield AI is a natural partner for his company because it shares the view that autonomous systems must be able to sense their environment to achieve their desired mission outcomes. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government and commercial customers around the globe,” he insisted.
According to Steele, Echodyne will continue to operate as a standalone entity, as a separate business unit within Shield AI’s mission systems business. Frankenberg will remain with the company, where he will report to Steele as part of its senior executive team. Echodyne is not going to layoff any staff, and nobody will be asked to relocate either, he said. In the longer term, the companies expect tighter integration of Echodyne’s radar systems with Shield AI’s drones.
The deal will see $4.8 billion paid out upon closing, with the other $500 million dependent on Echodyne meeting certain performance targets, which have not been disclosed. Shield AI said it was able to fund the deal with a combination of its own cash and a $2.5 billion cash injection that came via a Series H funding round led by Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase, which was also announced today.
Shield AI has a history of making decisive acquisitions. Its V-Bat and X-Bat drones are heavily based on technology developed by a company called Martin UAV Systems Inc. that it acquired in 2021. In June, it purchased Aechelon Technologies Inc., a developer of high-fidelity simulation and physics-based sensor modeling software, for an undisclosed price.
Steele added that the company may not be done with acquisitions, and will continue to look at making more deals in order to accelerate its growth strategy.

climate-energy-e03bb00576.headline: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
climate-energy-e03bb00576.fulltext:
Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
This guest post is by:
Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air
This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “flat or falling” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown.
Decline drivers
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “wasted” wind and solar fell.
Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.
The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates. This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.
Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.
The amount of electricity used by EVs grew by 53%, much faster than the number of EVs on the road, showing increased usage of the existing fleet in preference to fuelled vehicles.
Elsewhere, growth in the coal-to-chemical industry continued to slow down in the third quarter of 2026. The sector has been a key source of emissions growth, but high coal prices have weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand.
Finally, CO2 emissions from cement and steel production continued to fall in the third quarter, as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated.
Outlook for emissions
Energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has been robust.
This makes it likely that the growth in clean-power generation will exceed total energy demand growth this year, maintaining the structural fall in fossil-fuel use.
Looking ahead, this balance also relies on progress in removing barriers to new solar and wind power being added to the grid, which result in some clean electricity being “wasted”.
The recent slowdown in energy demand growth is partly – but not fully – explained by exceptionally mild weather in the third quarter.
Another key factor is weaker GDP growth. Since reported GDP growth remains within target, however, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus policies.
The focus of the economic stimulus announced to date is “six networks”, which includes the power grid and the transportation network.
These networks are highly relevant for energy and emissions – and they are already covered by policies that emphasise “green” and zero-carbon solutions.

work-careers-41dac2eae6.headline: Goldman Sachs bans non-engineers from using advanced AI tools
work-careers-41dac2eae6.fulltext:
Goldman Sachs has banned traders, bankers, and other staff from using advanced AI coding tools because of risk and productivity concerns.
The bank is limiting access to tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub to engineers and so-called “strats”—an investment banking term for workers who specialize in quantitative engineering and analytics—Bloomberg reported this week.
The move reportedly frustrated traders who used the tools to monitor data, build financial models, and produce graphics, among other things.
It also appears to undermine comments from Goldman chief information officer Marco Argenti in July, when he praised nontechnical staff using AI to build software prototypes before passing them to engineers for refinement.
A Goldman spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company allows staff to experiment with certain AI tools “to determine the best use cases across different parts of the firm” and to assess “a variety of factors including productivity and risk management.”
Once the experimental period ends, “we put [the tools] in the hands of those who are best suited to leverage them for the long term,” he said.
Fast Company reached out to Goldman Sachs for additional comment but had not heard back by the time of publication.

Meta buys AI coding startup Conductor as big tech races to lock in developers
Meta is acquiring AI coding startup Conductor, which lets developers control multiple AI coding agents at the same time. According to Axios, the acquisition is meant to strengthen Meta's AI developer products. Conductor CEO Charlie Holtz confirmed the deal in a blog post but didn't disclose a price.
The acquisition fits a broader trend. Because AI models are easily interchangeable, major AI companies are buying startups that build tooling around those models. The goal is to lock developers into their own platforms. Anthropic showed how valuable these tools can be with Claude Code, which hit an annualized revenue run rate of over $2.5 billion in February alone, according to Anthropic. In May, Anthropic also acquired Stainless.
On the same day as Meta, OpenAI announced plans to acquire Pierre Computer. SpaceX closed its $60 billion acquisition of Cursor in August. Software development is one of AI's most successful use cases and also helps improve the models themselves. Conductor Cloud shuts down on November 20, and the desktop app will stop receiving new models in early 2027.

ai-6dad7a604d.headline: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to bolster its AI infrastructure
ai-6dad7a604d.fulltext:
Dropbox is making a big push into AI infrastructure with a $350 million acquisition of cloud technology company Tigris Data, marking what appears to be its largest acquisition to date.
Announced Thursday, the deal is expected to strengthen Dropbox’s AI infrastructure capabilities and support the development of DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform aimed at businesses and developers building AI models and agents.
Dropbox told TechCrunch via email that the transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company also said it currently has no plans to reduce headcount as part of the acquisition. The company already cut 9% of its global workforce last month, WSJ reported.
DBX Agent Cloud will initially offer object storage as a stand-alone product, allowing businesses to purchase storage independently and use it with existing tools and applications built for Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), which is a cloud storage service that enables businesses to store and retrieve large volumes of data.
Beyond its infrastructure ambitions, Dropbox is also bringing more AI capabilities to its core product. Users will be able to ask AI to perform supported tasks using their files, choose between different AI models, and connect their Dropbox content to third-party tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse.
The company also plans to expand DBX Agent Cloud with additional capabilities designed to help AI systems work with different types of content, including documents, images, audio, and video. Other planned additions include filesystem features that will allow AI agents to manage files and maintain continuity across tasks and sessions.
Dropbox says the updated experience has already reached more than 70,000 teams. The initial rollout is available to eligible Standard and Advanced customers in the U.S., U.K., and Australia, with broader availability planned for 2027.
Tigris Data was founded by former Uber engineers who helped develop the ride-hailing company’s storage infrastructure. The company provides cloud storage technology that helps businesses store and access data across different regions. Its platform automatically positions data closer to the users and computing resources that need it, helping reduce access times and improve performance.
Tigris Data raised $25 million in a Series A funding round last year.
While the Tigris deal appears to be Dropbox’s largest acquisition, it is not the company’s first move to expand its AI capabilities through M&A. Dropbox has previously acquired several AI-focused companies, including Reclaim.ai, Promoted.ai, and Mobius Labs.

deep-tech-452ada200f.headline: Nvidia-Backed Agility Robotics Goes Public at $2.5B in Humanoid Robot Milestone
deep-tech-452ada200f.fulltext:
Nvidia-backed Agility Robotics goes public at a $2.5 billion valuation, raising $465 million in gross capital to expand its Digit humanoid robot business.
Agility Robotics’ Digit humanoid robots handle materials in a warehouse setting, demonstrating the potential of automated industrial operations. Image: Agility Robotics.
Humanoid robots have spent years learning to walk, lift, and work alongside humans. Now, they’re making their Wall Street debut.
Nvidia-backed Agility Robotics began trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 5 under the ticker AGLT, becoming what the company describes as the first US-listed, pure-play humanoid robotics business with proven commercial deployments. Its debut follows a $2.5 billion pre-money transaction valuation and approximately $465 million in gross capital from its merger and related financings.
Unlike many humanoid robots still confined to research labs and demonstrations, Agility’s Digit robots are already moving materials inside warehouses and manufacturing facilities. The company’s public listing marks a significant milestone for an industry racing to make advanced robotics commercially sustainable.
Agility completed its merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI on Nov. 4, clearing the way for its Nasdaq debut the following day.
The transaction valued Agility’s existing equity at approximately $2.5 billion, according to Bloomberg’s reporting. That pre-money transaction valuation should not be confused with the company’s market capitalization, which can fluctuate as its shares trade.
Rather than pursuing a traditional initial public offering, Agility used a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), a publicly traded entity created to merge with a private business and take it public.
According to Agility’s financing announcement, the merger and related financings provided approximately $465 million in gross capital before transaction expenses.
$201 million: A private investment in public equity (PIPE) led by Foxconn.
$100 million: Equity funding Agility had already received before the merger closed.
Because the $100 million was received earlier, the full $465 million should not be interpreted as new funding delivered on Nov. 5.
Agility plans to use the capital to expand manufacturing, increase commercial deployments, fulfill customer orders, and continue developing its humanoid robots.
As TechCrunch reported, the listing gives public-market investors an opportunity to evaluate a company focused specifically on commercial humanoid robotics, an industry where many prominent competitors remain privately held.
While many humanoid robot manufacturers attract attention with demonstrations of dancing, running, or acrobatics, Agility has taken a more practical approach.
Its flagship robot, Digit, is designed to perform repetitive physical tasks in warehouses, manufacturing facilities, and other industrial environments. The company says its robots have accumulated more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation, with deployments involving businesses such as GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Schaeffler.
At a GXO logistics facility in Georgia, Digit robots have moved more than 100,000 totes, demonstrating how humanoid machines can support existing warehouse operations.
Agility also announced an expansion of its partnership with GXO, with plans to deploy Digit at two additional US logistics facilities beginning in early 2027.
The company’s commercial strategy focuses on tasks that are physically demanding, repetitive, or difficult to staff consistently.
Agility’s approach could appeal to businesses looking to introduce automation without completely redesigning their facilities.
The company has also signed a commercial agreement with agricultural equipment manufacturer AGCO for a manufacturing pilot expected to begin in 2027. Three additional manufacturing customers are participating in paid programs, according to Agility.
These relationships suggest growing commercial interest, although pilot programs do not necessarily translate into large-scale orders.
Agility’s next major step is Digit 5, the latest generation of its humanoid robot.
Unveiled in September 2026, the updated machine is designed to perform a wider range of industrial tasks while operating more closely alongside human workers. According to Agility’s announcement, Digit 5 incorporates improvements in lifting, manipulation, safety, and battery technology.
The charging and productivity figures are development targets rather than independently verified results across large commercial fleets.
Agility is working with Nvidia and FORT Robotics on safety technologies intended to allow Digit 5 to operate closer to employees.
Some safety features remain under development, and Agility cautions that preliminary specifications and capabilities may change as the company continues to test and validate the platform.
The company has also partnered with Nyobolt on fast-charging battery technology intended to support longer operating periods.
Agility reports more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders for Digit 5. However, those commitments are conditional and should not be confused with completed sales or guaranteed revenue.
According to Agility’s SEC-filed investor presentation, the company’s earlier disclosures linked more than $300 million in committed orders to a three-year agreement for 1,000 Digit 5 robots with a single customer.
The company’s SEC prospectus identifies the customer involved in the May 2026 warrant arrangement as a related party. Under that arrangement, Agility agreed to issue warrants tied to the number of robots sourced, subject to the customer meeting a minimum commitment of 1,000 robots.
This distinction matters because transactions involving related parties can require additional scrutiny when assessing a company’s commercial traction and the independence of customer demand.
Agility repeated the $300 million-plus order figure in its announcement without providing an updated customer-by-customer breakdown. The commitments remain subject to contractual milestones and product requirements, meaning they should not be treated as guaranteed revenue.
The earlier disclosure also highlights the company’s reliance on a major customer agreement as it works to commercialize Digit 5.
Realizing the potential revenue will depend on Agility meeting contractual milestones, product features, specifications, and deployment requirements.
The company cautions in its SEC materials that committed orders may not ultimately convert into recognized revenue.
Agility expects to begin delivering Digit 5 to early-access customers in the first half of 2027, with broader availability targeted for the end of the year.
Tesla is developing its Optimus robot, Figure AI is pursuing industrial applications, and Boston Dynamics continues advancing its Atlas platform. Other companies, including Apptronik and several Chinese robotics manufacturers, are also working to commercialize humanoid machines.
The growing competition reflects expectations that humanoid robots could eventually become a major category of industrial automation. However, companies are pursuing different approaches to bringing the technology to market.
Some manufacturers emphasize advanced mobility, dexterity, and general-purpose capabilities. Others focus on narrower industrial applications that could generate revenue sooner. Agility has concentrated on the latter strategy, prioritizing repetitive workplace tasks that its robots can perform with existing technology.
Its commercial deployments may provide an advantage as businesses begin evaluating humanoid robots based on reliability, productivity, and cost rather than demonstrations alone.
The company’s Nasdaq listing also creates a new public-market reference point for the industry.
Unlike privately held competitors, Agility will face regular public financial reporting requirements, giving investors and industry observers greater visibility into its commercial progress.
Despite its commercial momentum, Agility remains in the early stages of building a sustainable business.
According to financial disclosures examined by Business Insider, the company generated approximately $1.8 million in revenue during 2025 while reporting a net loss of $138.1 million. More recent disclosures show that Agility generated approximately $174,000 in revenue during the first six months of 2026, compared with $625,000 during the same period in 2025.
According to MarketWatch, Agility reported an operating loss of approximately $362.7 million during the first half of 2026.
The figures illustrate the financial challenge facing a company investing heavily in technology and manufacturing while generating relatively limited commercial revenue.
Because the figures cover different reporting periods, the full-year 2025 net loss and first-half 2026 operating loss should not be interpreted as a direct year-over-year comparison. They also represent different accounting measures.
The first-half revenue figures show a substantial year-over-year decline. However, the company’s early-stage sales remain uneven, and individual robot sales or deployments can significantly affect results.
Agility’s reported operating loss also reflects substantial spending on research, development, and business operations, including noncash accounting expenses.

China’s second-largest contract chipmaker, Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor, is aggressively expanding into silicon photonics, as the company looks to capture the next wave of the global artificial intelligence infrastructure boom.
Speaking on an earnings call with analysts on Thursday, Hua Hong chairman and president Bai Peng said the company planned to significantly expand its footprint in silicon photonics – a critical technology used in AI optical modules – during its next major capacity expansion in 2027.
“We want to participate in all silicon-based devices [inside optical modules],” Bai said, adding the sector is one of the two areas – along with power management chips – in which it wants to add “significantly more capacity”.
The plan underscores how the chip foundry is seeking to capture the next wave of the AI hardware boom, as rising wafer prices and shipments helped it achieve robust earnings for the third quarter.
For the three months ended September 30, the Shanghai-based chipmaker’s net profit surged 147 per cent year on year to US$123.4 million, according to its stock exchange filing on Thursday.
Total revenue hit a record US$987.1 million, a nearly 20 per cent year-on-year increase. That was partly driven by the integration of its newly acquired subsidiary Huali Microelectronics, aimed at bolstering the company’s advanced manufacturing capacity.
Excluding the figures from Huali Microelectronics, the firm’s total revenue reached US$803.4 million, beating the company’s previous guidance of US$770 million to US$780 million.
Bai attributed the earnings surge to the ongoing AI boom, which has created a significant imbalance between chip supply and demand.
The AI boom had “caught most people by surprise”, Bai said. He likened the current AI infrastructure buildout to the early days of the internet, calling semiconductor chips “the new oil of the industrial age”.
“As a speciality technology foundry with a broad technology portfolio, Hua Hong Grace has seen increasingly higher demands for microcontrollers, flash memory, power management and power discrete products, with corresponding tight supply in some segments, even as we continue to expand capacity,” Bai said.
The chipmaker expected the pattern of rising demand and prices in the industry to continue “for some time”, he added.
To address a shortage in production capacity, the chipmaker is pushing forward with construction of its new Fab 9B facility “with highest possible speed”. It began moving equipment into the fab – based in the eastern Chinese city of Wuxi – in mid-September, he said.
However, the chipmaker anticipates ongoing supply constraints even as new capacity comes online, as local foundries – especially its larger rival Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC) – are running their fabs at full capacity amid a scramble among tech giants and start-ups to secure computing power.
A large part of the company’s capacity expansion for next year has already been booked by customers, Bai said, adding that the firm’s overall fab utilisation would remain at 100 per cent or slightly higher.
During the third quarter, Hua Hong’s total production capacity utilisation rate stood at 102.9 per cent, according to its filing on Thursday.
Shares of Hua Hong had dropped 2.04 per cent to HK$67.3 in Hong Kong ahead of the earnings release.

indian-startups-63bfec5390.headline: Spacetech Startup Cosmoserve Nets $6 Mn, Eyes Commercialisation By 2028
indian-startups-63bfec5390.fulltext: Cosmoserve Space has raised $6 Mn in a seed funding round led by Japan-based Rebright Partners. While Aranya Holdings and Naandi Ventures also participated in the round, existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC doubled down on their erstwhile bet. The startup shared plans to utilise the fresh capital to support tech demonstrations, fuel two upcoming missions, as well enhance the operations of its recently unveiled Hyderabad facility. Cosmoserve has now raised over $9 Mn since inception last year. The startup has doubled its valuation since it raised pre-seed funding in September, founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra told Inc42. The exact valuation is yet to be discerned. For context, the startup is building tech to remove defunct satellites and orbital debris from space and reduce the collision risks for operational spacecraft in a cost effective manner. It plans on optimising costs by setting up features within its craft that will allow it to refuel in-orbit and remove multiple pieces of debris in a single mission. The startup made its first tech demonstration, Mission Embrace-1, aboard Skyroot Aerospace’s Vikram-1 rocket. The mission was designed to test the startup’s soft robotic capture system that removes space debris, but the system’s robotic petals failed to deploy as intended. Cosmoserve claims to have now identified and addressed potential issues with the thermal mechanism used to release the petals and the impact of low temperatures on the system, according to Phanindra. The startup is now gearing up for Embrace-2, an upgraded version of the mission to validate its upgraded robotic capture mechanism, which is expected to launch in the coming months. It is also planning a full-scale demonstration of its debris-removal capabilities, aiming to break a world record by approaching within 10 m of a dead satellite. Phanindra, who served close to 15 years with the ISRO before setting up Cosmoserve in June 2025, believes that the startup would be able to complete all tech demos by 2027 and start commercial operations by 2028. “We have several letters of intent from satellite constellation operators – one from the US, one from Europe and two from India. They have to abide by the regulation for removing the dead satellite from space … so we are aiming to get one paid customer before actual commercial operations begin,” he added. Cosmoserve’s Base 1 Alongside the funding announcement, Cosmoserve inaugurated its new space debris removal facility in Hyderabad named Base 1 today, in an event attended by union minister of state Dr Jitendra Singh and Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu. Phanindra says that Base 1 is India’s first private and the world’s sixth facility equipped with space vision effects and microgravity simulation. In simpler terms, Base 1 can recreate conditions that spacecraft and equipment encounter in space, allowing companies to test how their tech will perform before an actual mission. This includes simulating how objects behave in microgravity (near-weightlessness) and how they appear or function under space-like visual conditions. This costs around ₹6 Cr to construct, per Phanindra. Base 1 houses infrastructure for designing, building and testing satellite servicing and space debris recovery missions. This includes an orbital rendezvous and capture lab, an ISO Class 8 clean room for satellite integration, a mission control centre and a microgravity simulation platform. The facility will also support the development of in-orbit satellite repair and refuelling technologies. Besides, the startup plans to use Base 1 to develop more critical technologies in-house in order to increase its share of local manufacturing from 60% and reduce dependence on imported components such as optics, avionics and space-grade electronics. “Primarily, the core technology we are building is a soft robotic capture system. We have a space robotics innovation lab where the R&D is happening. Then the next technology we are working on is a vision-based navigation system,” the founder told Inc42.

Bengaluru-based altM will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams.
Specialty chemicals startup altM has raised $10.3 million in a Series A funding round, with Rainmatter by Zerodha and Mela Ventures joining as new investors. Existing backers Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated in the round, along with strategic angel investors.
The Bengaluru-based company said it will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams. The investment will help altM transition from pilot-scale production to commercial manufacturing.
Founded in 2022 by Apoorv Garg and Yugal Raj Jain, altM uses lignocellulosic biomass, including sugarcane bagasse and rice straw, to produce industrial chemicals. Its processes use the cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin components of biomass to derive multiple products from a single feedstock.
The startup caters to industries such as beauty and personal care, textiles, construction, packaging and consumer goods, with a focus on developing bio-based alternatives to fossil-derived raw materials.
"We are pleased to partner with altM as they move into commercial-scale production. Re-wiring foundational supply chains away from fossil-derived inputs is one of the most critical challenges facing modern manufacturing today," said Abhinav Negi, Lead - Climate & DeepTech, Rainmatter by Zerodha.
"Solving DeepTech problems involves research and understanding interplay of multiple areas. altM is tackling one of the hardest problems in industrial chemistry which is creating new age materials that can match the performance of fossil-derived inputs while fundamentally changing where their carbon comes from," said Krishnakumar N, Managing Partner, Mela Ventures.
Since raising a $3.5 million seed round in 2023, altM has built an integrated research and pilot manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, bringing laboratory research, demonstration manufacturing and pilot production under one roof. The company said it has expanded its laboratory footprint nearly fivefold in less than two years, commissioned a demonstration manufacturing facility, and taken six molecules to demonstration scale. Of these, three have been selected for pilot plant production.
The products being prepared for commercialisation include a lignin-derived SPF booster for suncare, a cellulose-based rheology modifier, and bio-derived ferulic acid for cosmetics and personal care formulations.
"Industrial manufacturing has relied on fossil carbon for more than a century. We are building a new source of industrial carbon from agricultural residue," said Apoorv Garg, Co-founder and CEO of altM. "Our focus is on developing materials and manufacturing processes that allow customers to adopt these materials at the performance, cost, quality, and scale required for industrial applications."
"We've believed in altM from early on, and what makes us double down on our confidence is the team's ability to turn ambitious science into something real and commercially scalable. Going from the lab to reliable manufacturing and, ultimately, customers is a difficult journey. altM has shown a rare ability to make that transition," said Abhilash Sethi, Partner at Omnivore.

climate-energy-37addf8c27.headline: Renewable energy could save India $240 billion in coal, gas imports by 2030: IEA
climate-energy-37addf8c27.fulltext:
New Delhi: India's expanding renewable energy capacity could help the country save nearly USD 240 billion in cumulative coal and natural gas import expenditure by 2030, strengthening energy security and reducing exposure to international fuel price volatility, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The savings are expected to increase as solar and wind power displace imported fossil fuels, with annual savings projected to reach around USD 35 billion by 2030, exceeding India's actual non-coking coal and natural gas import bill in the financial year 2024-25.
In its 'India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026', the IEA said renewable electricity had already reduced cumulative spending on coal and natural gas imports by more than USD 100 billion between 2011 and 2025.
"Assuming fuel prices remain broadly consistent with average levels observed during 2024-2025, cumulative savings could approach USD 240 billion by 2030," the agency said.
Solar photovoltaic (PV) power is expected to account for the largest share of these savings, contributing approximately 60 per cent, while wind power is projected to contribute almost 30 per cent.
"Annual fossil fuel import savings are projected to reach approximately USD 35 billion by 2030, exceeding India's actual non-coking coal and natural gas import bill in FY 2024-25," the report said.
The agency highlighted that renewable energy expansion has already helped reduce India's dependence on imported coal. Without the solar PV, wind and bioenergy capacity added since 2010, coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million tonnes higher.
"Without the solar PV, wind and bioenergy capacity added since 2010, coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million tonnes higher and the import dependence of electricity generation would have exceeded 30%, approximately twice the actual level," the IEA said.
India's renewable power capacity is expected to reach around 530 GW by 2030, led by solar PV, which is projected to account for more than 350 GW. Wind capacity is expected to approach 90 GW, while hydropower capacity could reach 75 GW.
Renewable energy is also expected to account for 35 per cent of India's electricity generation by 2030, with output approaching 950 terawatt-hours, nearly double current levels.
However, the agency emphasised that continued investment in transmission infrastructure, energy storage and power system flexibility would be important to accommodate the growing share of variable renewable energy.
"These buffers become particularly valuable when supply disruptions and price spikes put fossil fuel markets under strain," the report said.

global-economics-b52c21410b.headline: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?
global-economics-b52c21410b.fulltext:
The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.
The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.
In the harsh blue light of Tuesday’s midterms, though, going all-in on Maga seems an unwisely unhedged bet. Democrats took decisive control of the US Congress, flipping seats right and left that in previous years seemed like given wins for Republicans. Governors’ mansions across the country likewise lit up blue as Democrats ascended even in the reddest of states, such as Texas.
Voters concerned about corruption expressed their displeasure at oligarchs’ blatant attempts to create a political environment to their liking. Voting against technocrats drove people into the hands of Democrats and away from Republicans. Tech oligarchs themselves, along with anger over the AI boom, datacenters and Flock surveillance cameras, shifted the tides.
“Voters rejected Republicans in part because they were bought and paid for by AI billionaires. Democrats must hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks,” wrote the Texas Democratic representative Greg Casar.
The Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff, who won re-election to the Senate, summed up the prevailing attitude towards the tech industry in his victory speech.
“The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction,” he said. He pledged to bring “big tech to heel”.
Others were more bellicose. Ed Markey, a Democratic senator from Massachusetts, tweeted late on Tuesday: “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”
Democrats have both promised congressional investigations into tech companies and moratoriums on datacenters, which may hamstring compute-hungry AI companies.
In the past year, the major AI firms have been competing in a fierce race to buy or build massive, noisy, resource-intensive facilities full of semiconductor chips that will supply their growing needs for computing power. Americans hate them. Democrats stand firmly in the way of that arms race. Democrats took governors’ mansions by promising to institute moratoriums on hyperscale datacenter construction.
Gina Hinojosa of Texas, Amy Acton of Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia have all pledged pauses.
Then there are the promised investigations. Letters to preserve records for future investigations have already gone out to Nvidia and Amazon. Tech was the villain of the midterms. Angry constituents want to see it penalized. Elon Musk presents a meaty target as the billionaire most closely allied with the Trump administration and the richest man in the world. Investigating his conduct with the “department of government efficiency”, which laid waste to the humanitarian agency USAID and wide swaths of the US government, will be a political lay-up for Democrats newly in control and desiring a public spectacle.
Musk had the worst night of anyone but Trump on Tuesday. The world’s richest man gave $450m in support of Republican candidates, most of all to Ken Paxton in Texas, but he reaped little, if any, reward. Paxton lost by a major margin. Musk remained silent for about eight hours as results poured in, each piece of news more disastrous for his rightwing project than the last. In what seemed like capitulation, he deleted a Tuesday tweet that read: “Vote red today!”
By Wednesday morning, the SpaceX CEO wanted off the planet. “Datacenters in space are looking pretty good right now,” he wrote.
He may not get the chance to set up his orbital computers. Democrats may likewise investigate or attempt to unwind the multibillion-dollar merger of SpaceX and Musk’s AI company, xAI, which makes the Nazi-friendly nudification bot Grok. xAI has a $200m contract with the US military, which likewise seems like an easy win for Democrats to meddle with.
Mark Zuckerberg may feel deja vu when he finds himself sitting across the table from an inquisition, as he repeatedly did at the end of the 2010s. The Meta CEO made a nakedly political pivot under Trump 2.0 with his shift to the right. He appeared at Mar-a-Lago to show off Meta’s camera-equipped glasses to Trump and axed his company’s vaunted diversity, equity and inclusion program as the president waged war on DEI.
Already the most disliked man in America, Zuckerberg will show with his next era whether he believes in anything as much as he does power. Was his interest in jiu-jitsu mixed martial arts authentic or a way to ingratiate himself with the manosphere’s podcast hosts? We may know by the time he faces his first inquest. Perhaps he’ll return to the liberal roots of his former public image like founding a pro-immigration non-profit, as he did a decade ago.
Meanwhile, OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, himself seen at Mar-a-Lago, appears in damage control mode on Tuesday. His tweet on Tuesday night read like a Bernie Sanders talking point: “People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress.” Inviting human-first regulation, Altman appeared to be trying to distance himself from Trump’s free-for-all stance, and the president’s recent efforts to rebrand AI as “superintelligence”.
But the billionaires of Silicon Valley seem unlikely to rehabilitate their public images overnight after years of pandering only to power brokers. They have little to say on the issues of the day: affordability and corruption. The majority of Americans see them as avatars of extreme wealth inequality and cynical, pay-to-play politics. What can a billionaire offer a populace angry about prices?

work-careers-7a0a6519e1.headline: Apple is slashing AI budgets—the latest company to do so
work-careers-7a0a6519e1.fulltext:
Tokenmaxxing is on the way out, even as some of the biggest players in the tech industry are urging their employees to use AI as much as possible. A new Bloomberg report reveals that Apple is cutting employee budgets for AI token usage while remaining just as committed to deploying AI to boost efficiency.
Apple has already reduced the daily spending limit from $300 to $200 for certain engineers, according to Bloomberg, but the company reportedly plans to cut that down even more. Sources told Bloomberg that the daily cap could drop as low as $100 for some engineering teams. In many other departments, daily AI spending is already capped at $100; now Apple is considering reducing the limit to $25 for certain teams.
The spending limit is measured in tokens, which are units of AI usage that represent fragments of text or data processed by AI systems.
This move comes as Apple continues pressing its engineers and other employees to use AI more in day-to-day operations. But it also reflects a larger trend rippling across the tech industry, as companies struggle to justify their outsize spending on artificial intelligence.
After pushing their employees to adopt AI, many tech employers seem to be grappling with the fact that those investments have not yielded the productivity gains that they anticipated.
According to Bloomberg, some Apple employees believed many people weren’t making use of the $300 limit and that it was higher than needed. But other employees seemed to view it as a sign that Apple is looking to reduce costs—and that the company could resort to layoffs.
Bloomberg reports that Apple is already taking steps to streamline its operations in the interest of maximizing efficiency, and recently appointed CEO John Ternus is reportedly already advocating for reducing layers of management (something that Amazon has also sought to do over the last year).

world-c9fe0405c6.headline: Investors wipe US$2.5 trillion off Nasdaq as Democratic sweep prompts AI fears
world-c9fe0405c6.fulltext:

Big tech stocks slumped on Thursday in their biggest decline since ⁠the “Liberation Day” rout last year, extending what has ⁠been a punishing autumn for the AI trade.
The Nasdaq 100 index ⁠was set for market value declines exceeding US$2 trillion on investor fears that the Democratic Party’s sweeping midterm victory could stall AI infrastructure expansion and force a chaotic reckoning for smaller firms whose capacity to raise funds has already been limited by higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions.
Analysts and portfolio managers said declines in once-hot areas such as semiconductors and AI infrastructure were not entirely surprising, given the scale of earlier gains in many of these stocks and the financing concerns that have ‌shadowed the so-called neoclouds, smaller infrastructure firms such as Nebius and CoreWeave, since US interest rates rose late in the summer.
Shares of semiconductor and neocloud companies posted the most significant declines, reflecting worries that data centre buildouts worth billions of dollars could face delays.
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index fell as much as 11.2 per cent to touch its lowest level in more than six months. Nvidia dropped 9 per cent and Advanced Micro slumped 15 per cent.
Many analysts said the scale of the declines, which have now extended into a second straight day, suggests sentiment is changing, which could portend further selling, probably starting with Friday’s market sessions in Asia.
Japan’s Nikkei and Korea’s Kospi have risen strongly this year, both up more than 20 per cent, but ⁠they declined significantly following Wednesday’s Wall Street rout and might be expected to do the same on Friday.
“Despite the magnitude of today’s move, volatility has not yet reached the capitulation or contrarian extremes ‌historically associated with capitulation points,” said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial in Charlotte, North Carolina.
Hyperscalers, which defied Wednesday’s broad tech sell-off, also dropped. Amazon.com fell 2.5 per cent and Alphabet slid 2 per cent.
The selling suggests investors are starting to account for the unpopularity of the data centre ‌buildout, with some sceptics saying the costs it has imposed on US communities have yet to be fully considered.
“There’s going to be a lot of pushback ⁠about those data centres being geographically located in ⁠someone’s backyard, straining the power grid, straining the water systems,” said Bruce Zaro, managing director at Granite Wealth Management in Plymouth, Massachusetts.
“Although there are a number of data centres already approved, there are still a lot to be permitted. There’s going to ‌be a difficult road to get those permitted forthcoming.”
Around 30 per cent of expected US data centre capacity additions in 2028 could be at risk from potential construction pauses, UBS analysts estimated, highlighting the threat to an industry whose growth depends on a rapid ‌buildout of ‌new facilities.
The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worries about the return on investment for the enormous sums being poured into the technology.
CoreWeave, which has become a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending and the need shared by many of these companies to regularly access market financing, slumped 10 per cent.
Its five-year credit ⁠default spreads, which measure market expectations of a potential default, widened to a record high, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data.
Nebius, another neocloud company, dropped 15 per cent. Shares of both firms have ⁠dropped by half or more since the Nasdaq Composite hit a record on October 6.
The sharp declines put the Nasdaq Composite on track to enter correction territory, defined as a 10 per cent drop from its recent peak. The Nasdaq 100 was last down 5.9 per cent.
“The market’s moving from the promise of AI to the price of AI,” said ‌Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline Investment Management.
“There’s ‌no question that AI is going to be transformative for the world in the long run. But that doesn’t mean every AI-related stock is currently priced appropriately. There’s going to be a lot of turmoil.”
Data centre operators Applied Digital, Cipher Digital and IREN tumbled more than 14 per cent each.
The weakness extended to utilities and equipment suppliers exposed to the buildout. GE Vernova fell about 6 per cent, while Constellation Energy slipped 3 per cent.
Microsoft declined 2 per cent. The company is tightening oversight of some data centre projects from Nebius, IREN and Nscale, Bloomberg News reported.

indian-startups-c24a726edb.headline: CERT-In warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-driven attacks
indian-startups-c24a726edb.fulltext:
An advisory from the government body said the AI-assisted financial threat is still active and warns BFSI entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has issued an advisory warning that hackers are attacking non-banking financial corporations with the help of artificial intelligence.
Terming the threat campaign "CRAFTY FALCON", the government body describes it as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor that surveys its targets with machine intelligence, operates at machine speed and strikes by invoking the victim's own payment and disbursement APIs.”
CERT-In is the national nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents.
“Continued analysis of incidents reported by affected entities including non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment aggregators, payment service providers and cryptocurrency exchanges / virtual digital asset service providers has revealed a significant escalation of this campaign.”
The advisory further said the threat is still active and has warned BFSI (banking, financial services, and insurance) entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
Outlining some of the reported attacks, the advisory said merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators were exploited or abused to move funds. Cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers were also targeted, with wallet keys stolen and funds siphoned from cryptocurrency wallets.
The body also revealed that its analysis has shown the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools. These include the ARTEX family of LLM-based, the PentAGI autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework.
Last month, CERT-In had flagged incidents involving AI agents exceeding their authorised tasks and accessing live systems of Indian organisations, alongside financially motivated attacks using open-source agentic AI tools.
Globally too, such attacks have been on the rise. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported observing AI offensive security tools being used in real-world intrusions, including attacks on organisations across the United States and Europe.

climate-energy-6a9163c849.headline: India plans energy storage mandate for state utilities amid power shortages
climate-energy-6a9163c849.fulltext:
India plans to make state power utilities install energy storage capacity as the government seeks to reduce electricity shortages during evening and night-time hours, when solar power generation falls even as demand remains high.
Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal announced the proposed requirement at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit on Thursday. The move is aimed at allowing utilities to store surplus clean electricity generated during the day and use it when demand peaks later in the day.
The government has not yet decided how much storage capacity state utilities will be required to install or provided a timeline for implementing the mandate. Agarwal said the situation was still evolving and added that more clean energy tenders linked to energy storage were in the works.
The announcement comes as India grapples with a growing mismatch between renewable energy generation and electricity demand. Despite having more than 300 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil fuel-based power generation capacity, the country has continued to rely on coal-fired plants to meet demand during evening and night-time hours.
The lack of adequate battery storage has made it difficult for state utilities to store surplus electricity generated during periods of high solar output and release it when renewable generation declines.
India's power system faces a growing challenge as solar and wind generation expand. Solar power generation is concentrated during daylight hours, while electricity consumption often remains high after sunset. Without adequate storage, surplus daytime electricity cannot be shifted to periods when demand is higher and solar generation is unavailable.
The supply gap has increased pressure on conventional power sources, particularly coal-fired plants.
India's electricity shortages reached 560 million kilowatt-hours in September, the highest level since August 2023, according to government data reported by Reuters. Coal-fired power generation rose 25.7 per cent year-on-year in October, its fastest annual increase in three years, while hydropower generation declined 26 per cent amid weaker rainfall.
The proposed mandate follows the Union Cabinet's approval on Wednesday of a Rs 14,500-crore viability gap funding (VGF) scheme to develop 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage capacity between FY27 and FY31.
The programme will support 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage projects, 30 GWh of battery energy storage systems and 2 GWh of emerging storage technologies. The projects are expected to attract a total investment of Rs 97,600 crore.
Under the scheme, public and private sector electricity distribution companies will be eligible for financial support for battery storage and pumped hydro projects. The government has also introduced a minimum domestic content requirement of 40 per cent for battery energy storage projects to encourage local manufacturing and reduce dependence on imported components.
Battery storage systems can absorb surplus electricity when solar generation is high and release it when demand increases. Pumped hydro storage works by using surplus electricity to pump water to an upper reservoir, which can then be released through turbines to generate power when needed.
The government estimates that the additional capacity supported by the scheme will help India move towards its requirement of 411 GWh of grid-scale energy storage by 2031-32.
The storage push is part of a wider effort to strengthen India's electricity infrastructure as renewable power capacity expands. The government is targeting 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based installed power capacity by 2030.
The International Energy Agency (IEA), in its India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026 released on November 3, said India's renewable power capacity had crossed 300 GW in 2026, almost quadrupling over the past decade. The country also achieved its target of sourcing 50 per cent of installed power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
The IEA expects India's renewable power capacity to reach around 530 GW by 2030, with solar power accounting for more than 80 per cent of new additions. However, the agency cautioned that the expansion would require faster investment in electricity grids, energy storage and system flexibility.
India is also planning to make battery storage mandatory for new government-backed solar and wind projects from July 2027, according to draft regulations reported by Reuters in September.

China has blocked the sale of ABB’s robotics unit to SoftBank Group, dealing a blow to the Japanese investment firm’s plans to expand into physical AI.
A Chinese government agency blocked the $5.4 billion deal, ABB said in an emailed statement. The takeover was widely expected to bolster SoftBank’s revenue and profit while it awaits a boost from OpenAI’s public debut.
SoftBank’s shares were down around 7% in Tokyo on Thursday. A company spokesperson declined to comment.
Founder Masayoshi Son has listed the deal as a key part of his ambition to play a larger role in the artificial intelligence buildout. The Tokyo-based firm was looking to take over a business from Swiss-Swedish conglomerate ABB with more than 7,000 employees, which supplies robotic arms and industrial machinery to manufacturers like BMW and has a large presence in China.
Investors worry about Son’s commitments to AI, from SoftBank’s near-$65 billion bet on OpenAI to pledges of hundreds of billions of dollars on data center projects. Some had looked to ABB’s expected contribution to SoftBank’s bottom line for assurance that the company was not overextending itself.
“ABB Robotics lacks the cutting-edge innovation found across SoftBank’s physical AI startup portfolio, but its domain expertise and manufacturing knowhow had been expected to transform robotic concepts into actual businesses,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kirk Boodry.
Beijing’s move against the ABB deal casts more uncertainty over SoftBank’s ambitions, and reflects the Chinese government’s renewed emphasis on safeguarding its data and technology in the AI era.
In April, China’s powerful National Development and Reform Commission blocked Meta Platforms’s $2 billion acquisition of agentic AI startup Manus, issuing a one-line notice saying it had decided to prohibit foreign investment in the startup in accordance with laws and regulations.
SoftBank’s acquisition was similarly subjected to a foreign investment security review by the state planner, according to an earlier report in the Financial Times. China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review prohibited the deal, according to the ABB statement.
Beijing, recognizing how data is the foundation of artificial intelligence, has this year clamped down on the transfer of vital information abroad. That’s true also of the robotics arena, where data is fundamental to eventually making robots work.
Japan is home to many of the world’s biggest industrial robot makers including Fanuc, Yaskawa Electric and Kawasaki Heavy Industries. Most have partnered with Nvidia to explore ways to use AI inside factories, hospitals and logistics networks and stay ahead of rising competition from China.

deep-tech-82ef1fda09.headline: China Blocks SoftBank’s $5.4 Billion ABB Robotics Deal Over AI Data Concerns
deep-tech-82ef1fda09.fulltext:
China blocked SoftBank’s $5.4 billion acquisition of ABB’s robotics division, citing national-security concerns over Chinese operations, robotics data, and potential AI applications, underscoring increasing regulatory scrutiny of cross-border technology transactions.
China has blocked SoftBank’s proposed $5.4 billion acquisition of ABB’s robotics division, dealing a setback to Masayoshi Son’s ambitions in artificial intelligence and industrial automation. ABB confirmed the prohibition on November 5, 2026, highlighting Beijing’s willingness to intervene in transactions between foreign companies when Chinese technology, operations and sensitive data are involved.
The decision underscores the growing importance of data in national-security reviews. According to reporting first published by the Financial Times, Chinese officials were concerned that robotics information generated domestically could move overseas and help train foreign AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, a major SoftBank investment.
ABB said China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review prohibited the transaction. Earlier reporting identified scrutiny by the National Development and Reform Commission, China’s state planning agency, which reviews foreign investments with potential national-security implications.
The reported concern went beyond ownership of robotic machinery. Industrial automation generates information about how machines operate in factories, interact with equipment and perform manufacturing tasks. Access to that experience can support the development of AI systems capable of operating in the physical world. Reporting on the decision identified overseas transfers of robotics data as a central issue.
However, concerns about specific transfers remain reported regulatory reasoning—not evidence that SoftBank or ABB had already improperly exported information. The available accounts do not establish that such a transfer occurred.
SoftBank announced the acquisition in October 2025, with completion originally expected in mid-to-late 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. The deal would have brought a robotics business employing more than 7,000 people into Son’s expanding AI portfolio.
ABB Robotics supplies industrial robotic arms and automation equipment to manufacturers including BMW. Its established customer relationships and production expertise offered SoftBank something different from an investment in an early-stage AI company: an existing platform for deploying technology commercially.
Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kirk Boodry said ABB’s domain knowledge and manufacturing capabilities were expected to help transform SoftBank’s robotics concepts into operating businesses. The acquisition therefore represented a bridge between AI research and practical industrial deployment.
China is ABB’s largest robotics market. Approximately 90% of the machines supplied to Chinese customers are manufactured locally, and the company employs thousands of people in the country. Those operations help explain why Chinese approval mattered despite the buyer and seller being headquartered abroad.
ABB Engineering in Shanghai also hosts the group’s global robotics headquarters and serves as an important research, development and production centre. The transaction consequently involved substantial capabilities embedded within China’s industrial ecosystem.
ABB said it remained in close dialogue with SoftBank and was continuing to work on the transaction. Reporting indicated that SoftBank was examining whether approval could be sought again, but no revised structure or successful regulatory remedy had been announced.
The immediate lesson for investors is that AI acquisitions increasingly face scrutiny over expertise and information—not simply market concentration. China’s decision shows how domestic operations can give a government influence over a global technology transaction.

ai-e86427d201.headline: Dropbox Plans $350M AI Infrastructure Deal With Tigris Buy, Its Biggest Acquisition Yet
ai-e86427d201.fulltext:
Dropbox announced Thursday plans to acquire Tigris Data for $350 million in a transaction the company told Crunchbase News would mark its largest acquisition since its founding in 2007.
Founded by former Uber engineers, Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris is building a network of localized data storage centers that it claims can meet the distributed compute needs of modern AI workloads.
Tigris has raised about $31.9 million since its founding in 2021, per Crunchbase data. Its October 2025 Series A brought in $25 million from lead investor Spark Capital, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and Basis Set Ventures, which also led its seed round. Other earlier backers include General Catalyst.
Co-founder and CEO Ovais Tariq told TechCrunch at the time of its Series A that the startup had grown 8x every year since its founding in November 2021.
The planned deal would give Dropbox a storage platform built for developers whose applications run across multiple cloud providers.
A push into AI infrastructure
The acquisition news coincides with what San Francisco-based Dropbox describes as “a significant shift” in its AI strategy as it expands beyond storing and sharing files into selling the infrastructure that companies use to build AI applications.
Publicly traded Dropbox also unveiled DBX Agent Cloud, which will initially offer standalone object storage — a way to store and retrieve large collections of data, including images, video and the files used to train and run AI models.
For Dropbox, buying Tigris offers a faster route into a market that serves a different audience from the individuals and businesses that use its file-sharing software.
“Tigris brings together a product already running in production, an experienced team, and established relationships with AI developers,” Eric Webster, Dropbox’s chief business officer, told Crunchbase News via email. “That combination would accelerate our entry into infrastructure for AI applications through DBX Agent Cloud.”
A bigger bet amid a slower deal pace
Dropbox has made 35 known acquisitions, according to Crunchbase, with much of that activity taking place in its earlier years. Between 2012 and 2015, the company conducted 23 publicly reported acquisitions, including nine in 2014 alone. In contrast, it made four acquisitions across 2024 and 2025, averaging two per year, roughly 65% below its earlier pace.
Its recent purchases suggest a focus on AI-powered productivity, search and security. Dropbox acquired scheduling startup Reclaim.ai and document security company Nira in 2024, followed by Promoted.ai and Mobius Labs in 2025.
While the planned Tigris purchase would be its largest yet, Dropbox has made other sizable purchases over time. Its acquisitions of e-signature company HelloSign in 2019, document-sharing platform DocSend in 2021 and business forms provider FormSwift in 2022 had purchase prices of $230 million, $165 million and $95 million, respectively.
Two paths into AI
Dropbox’s push into AI infrastructure is one part of a broader strategy that also includes adding AI capabilities to its existing file-sharing product.
For existing customers, the company is bringing AI directly to their Dropbox files to help them find, understand, create, edit and organize content, according to Webster. Customers can switch between supported AI models and work with their Dropbox files in tools like ChatGPT and Claude, with results returning to Dropbox.
For companies and developers, meanwhile, DBX Agent Cloud extends Dropbox’s storage capabilities to the infrastructure behind AI applications and agents.
“DBX Agent Cloud opens a new developer and infrastructure market for Dropbox, while AI inside Dropbox is intended to deepen engagement, retention and expansion among existing customers,” Webster said.

india-deep-tech-7f77597ae4.headline: Startup bringing AI-powered robotics to the cath lab raises $160M from GE HealthCare, other investors
india-deep-tech-7f77597ae4.fulltext:
Laza Medical, a California-based medtech company, has raised up to $160 million in new Series B financing led by GE HealthCare. Additional investors included Unorthodox Ventures, PA MedTech, and AMED.
Laza Medical is a privately held portfolio company of Shifamed, a California-based medical innovation hub founded by entrepreneur Amr Salahieh. Salahieh also serves as the founder and chairman of the board of Laza Medical.
Laza Medical is focused on developing artificial intelligence (AI)-powered robotic imaging technologies for the cath lab. The company’s flagship product, the Laza Medical System, is being developed to help clinicians perform structural heart, electrophysiology and diagnostic procedures in the cath lab. Its advanced AI algorithms provide a real-time view of the patient’s heart. In addition, the technology is being built to guide the user through each and every step thanks to echocardiography-based tracking capabilities.
The company previously secured $36 million in financing back in December 2023. GE HealthCare was involved with that funding round as well.
“The cath lab is poised for a fundamental evolution, and intelligent imaging powered by AI will play a defining role in what comes next,” Salahieh said in a statement. “As we reimagine the role of imaging in interventional care, we are grateful for the strong support from our investors, which validates our approach and reinforces our conviction that this solution will streamline processes, reduce variability, and ultimately improve the quality and reach of cardiac procedures.”
“The future of cardiac intervention must be one where access, consistency, and quality of care are no longer barriers to better outcomes,” added Jyoti Gera, CEO of cardiovascular and interventional solutions at GE HealthCare. “Integrating imaging modalities so they work seamlessly together has the potential to redefine the cath lab, enabling more efficient workflows today and paving the way for smarter, robotic procedures tomorrow. We’re excited to expand our collaboration with Laza and work together toward this shared vision.”
Michael has more than 19 years of experience as a professional writer and editor. He has written at length about cardiology, radiology, artificial intelligence and other key healthcare topics.
