While Aranya Holdings and Naandi Ventures also participated in the round, existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC doubled down on their erstwhile bet. The startup shared plans to utilise the fresh capital to support tech demonstrations, fuel two upcoming missions, as well enhance the operations of its recently unveiled Hyderabad facility. Cosmoserve has now raised over $9 Mn since inception last year. The startup has doubled its valuation since it raised pre-seed funding in September, founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra told Inc42. The exact valuation is yet to be discerned. For context, the startup is building tech to remove defunct satellites and orbital debris from space and reduce the collision risks for operational spacecraft in a cost effective manner. It plans on optimising costs by setting up features within its craft that will allow it to refuel in-orbit and remove multiple pieces of debris in a single mission. The startup made its first tech demonstration, Mission Embrace-1, aboard Skyroot Aerospace’s Vikram-1 rocket. The mission was designed to test the startup’s soft robotic capture system that removes space debris, but the system’s robotic petals failed to deploy as intended. Cosmoserve claims to have now identified and addressed potential issues with the thermal mechanism used to release the petals and the impact of low temperatures on the system, according to Phanindra. The startup is now gearing up for Embrace-2, an upgraded version of the mission to validate its upgraded robotic capture mechanism, which is expected to launch in the coming months. It is also planning a full-scale demonstration of its debris-removal capabilities, aiming to break a world record by approaching within 10 m of a dead satellite. Phanindra, who served close to 15 years with the ISRO before setting up Cosmoserve in June 2025, believes that the startup would be able to complete all tech demos by 2027 and start commercial operations by 2028. “We have several letters of intent from satellite constellation operators – one from the US, one from Europe and two from India. They have to abide by the regulation for removing the dead satellite from space … so we are aiming to get one paid customer before actual commercial operations begin,” he added. Cosmoserve’s Base 1 Alongside the funding announcement, Cosmoserve inaugurated its new space debris removal facility in Hyderabad named Base 1 today, in an event attended by union minister of state Dr Jitendra Singh and Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu. Phanindra says that Base 1 is India’s first private and the world’s sixth facility equipped with space vision effects and microgravity simulation. In simpler terms, Base 1 can recreate conditions that spacecraft and equipment encounter in space, allowing companies to test how their tech will perform before an actual mission. This includes simulating how objects behave in microgravity (near-weightlessness) and how they appear or function under space-like visual conditions. This costs around ₹6 Cr to construct, per Phanindra. Base 1 houses infrastructure for designing, building and testing satellite servicing and space debris recovery missions. This includes an orbital rendezvous and capture lab, an ISO Class 8 clean room for satellite integration, a mission control centre and a microgravity simulation platform. The facility will also support the development of in-orbit satellite repair and refuelling technologies. Besides, the startup plans to use Base 1 to develop more critical technologies in-house in order to increase its share of local manufacturing from 60% and reduce dependence on imported components such as optics, avionics and space-grade electronics. “Primarily, the core technology we are building is a soft robotic capture system. We have a space robotics innovation lab where the R&D is happening. Then the next technology we are working on is a vision-based navigation system,” the founder told Inc42.

However, the robotic capture petals did not deploy as planned, providing the company with data for further development.

Cosmoserve plans to test its robotic capture systems through microgravity flights, reflight Mission Embrace and conduct a full-scale space debris capture demonstration in 2027.

india-deep-tech-6af3b60562.headline: Zipline Hits $21.5B Valuation as Walmart Takes Drone Delivery Nationwide

Zipline Hits $21.5B Valuation as Walmart Takes Drone Delivery Nationwide
November 5, 2026
Zipline (Techstars 2011) has raised $1.5B at a $21.5B valuation and signed a new multi-year deal with Walmart to add 300 drone delivery sites across the U.S.
Zipline (Techstars 2011) has raised $1.5B at a $21.5B valuation and signed a new multi-year agreement with Walmart to add 300 drone delivery sites across the U.S., TechCrunch reports.
The company plans to use the new capital to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire the workforce needed to build a nationwide drone delivery network.
A Bigger Bet From Walmart
Zipline and Walmart have been delivering by drone together since 2021 and currently operate 21 active sites. The new agreement adds 300 more, a roughly fifteenfold jump that puts drone delivery within reach of far more Walmart shoppers across the country.
Momentum is already building. Zipline says its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October 2026, and the new funding is designed to push that number higher.
From Blood Deliveries in Rwanda to Backyards Across America
Zipline launched in 2014 by delivering blood to hospitals in Rwanda, then expanded into Ghana and Nigeria. Its first U.S. operation came in 2020, carrying medical equipment and supplies for Novant Health in North Carolina. Two years later, Zipline earned Part 135 air carrier certification from the FAA, clearing the way for long-range commercial drone deliveries.
Today, Zipline delivers food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several U.S. cities, and Japan. Earlier this year, it also partnered with Uber to bring drone delivery to more customers.
How Zipline Flies
Zipline runs two drone platforms built for different jobs.
- Platform 2 handles home delivery, carrying up to eight pounds within a 10-mile radius.
- Platform 1 serves enterprise, business, and government customers with long-range flights of up to 120 miles round trip.
A Techstars Story That Started With Robots
Zipline’s Techstars roots go back to the fall of 2011, when the founding team joined Techstars Seattle. Back then, the company was called Romotive and focused on turning smartphones into robots. What stood out to the Techstars Seattle team was the founders’ passion for what they were building and their ability to take feedback well.
That’s the kind of team Techstars bets on early. Fifteen years later, Zipline is building one of the most ambitious logistics networks in the world.
Read the full story on TechCrunch, and learn more about Zipline at flyzipline.com.

indian-startups-133b72fdf2.headline: Specialty chemicals startup altM raises $10.3 Mn led by Rainmatter, Mela Ventures
indian-startups-133b72fdf2.fulltext:
Bengaluru-based specialty chemicals startup altM has raised $10.3 million in a Series A funding round led by new investors Rainmatter by Zerodha and Mela Ventures. The round also saw participation from existing investors Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact, along with VC Grid and strategic angel investors.
The company will use the fresh capital to expand its manufacturing capabilities, research and development, customer qualification programmes, and engineering and commercial teams as it moves from pilot-scale production to commercial manufacturing.
Founded in 2022 by former Tesla manufacturing leaders Apoorv Garg and Yugal Raj Jain, altM is developing a specialty chemicals platform that converts agricultural residue into high-performance industrial chemicals. Bioprocessing scientist Dr Harshad Velankar later joined the company as its chief scientific officer.
The company's platform converts lignocellulosic biomass, including sugarcane bagasse and rice straw, into materials for beauty and personal care, textiles, industrial chemicals, construction, packaging and consumer goods.
It uses cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin to produce multiple products from a single feedstock. The process enables agricultural residue to serve as a source of industrial carbon and reduces dependence on fossil-derived raw materials.
Since raising $3.5 million in a seed round in 2023, altM has built an integrated R&D and pilot manufacturing facility in Bengaluru. The facility brings laboratory research, demonstration manufacturing and pilot production under one roof.
The company has expanded its laboratory footprint nearly fivefold, commissioned its demonstration manufacturing facility and advanced six molecules to demonstration scale. Three of these have been selected for pilot plant production.
Its first products moving towards commercialisation include a lignin-derived SPF booster for suncare applications, a cellulose-based rheology modifier and bio-derived ferulic acid for cosmetics and personal care formulations.
altM competes with Scimplifi, Covvalent, Atomgrid and Tulon Materials, which have also raised fresh funding this year.
The latest funding will help altM scale its manufacturing operations and expand customer deployments as it seeks to build a platform for producing industrial chemicals from agricultural residue.

india-deep-tech-b4dda4ff48.headline: Zipline is expanding Walmart drone delivery after funding that values it at $21.5 billion
india-deep-tech-b4dda4ff48.fulltext:
Zipline announced a $1.5 billion raise on Thursday at a $21.5 billion post-money valuation, and the drone delivery company is adding 300 Walmart $WMT -1.12% sites under a new multi-year agreement.
Paradigm, WCM Investment Management and Layer Global led the round, the company said. Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber $UBER -1.56%, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest and Salesforce $CRM -2.07% Ventures also took part. Zipline brought in over $600 million in January when it was valued at $7.6 billion, according to Bloomberg.
Zipline will use the money to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and increase hiring as it builds a nationwide drone delivery network, the company said.
Walmart announced the agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites nationwide, with potential to expand further. Walmart's drone program has completed more than 2 million deliveries, and the retailer has worked with Zipline on drone deliveries since 2021, the company said. Tens of thousands of eligible items can be delivered in as fast as 30 minutes where the service is available, Walmart said.
Zipline and Walmart operate 21 sites in Texas and Arkansas, and the drones carry packages weighing up to 8 pounds, according to Bloomberg. Walmart also has a separate drone delivery arrangement with Alphabet $GOOGL -2.20%-owned Wing.
“We see customers try drone delivery for the novelty and then continue to come back to it for the convenience when they need something in minutes,” Greg Cathey, Walmart’s senior vice president of e-commerce fulfillment transformation, said in a statement.
Zipline founder and Chief Executive Officer Keller Cliffton told Bloomberg Television: “I think both we and they have been quite startled by the level of customer demand.” He added: “We are going to expand to every metro and then eventually every home in the U.S.”
Uber is targeting 1 million deliveries a day with Zipline by 2029, Zipline said. The company said its drones made more than 1 million deliveries in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex this year. In October, the median Zipline order arrived 19 minutes after checkout, compared with more than 30 minutes for traditional delivery, the company said.
Zipline said a group of its longest-tenured restaurant partners saw a 26% increase in delivery gross merchandise value, with 80% of the increase coming from Zipline orders.

global-economics-60e85553bc.headline: US stock market crash: Chip stocks extend sell-off, AMD, Arm, Qualcomm and Sandisk plunge up to 17%; Nasdaq down 6%

A KsheerasagarUpdated5 Nov 2026, 11:26 PM IST Chip stocks came under renewed selling pressure in Thursday's trade, extending previous day sell-off, with AMD, Arm Holdings, Qualcomm, Micron Technology and Sandisk leading the declines. The stocks fell between 9% and 17% amid concerns that a Democrat-led Congress could push for tighter restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and data centre development. Disappointing reactions to earnings and business outlooks from Arm Holdings and Qualcomm added to the selling pressure. Qualcomm shares plunged 14% after investors were disappointed with the company's profit forecast, while Arm Holdings (ARM) dropped 15% after the chip designer's revenue guidance failed to impress Wall Street. Micron Technology was another major laggard, falling 13% after the memory chipmaker paused plans for a Taiwanese plant amid labour disputes. Following a 7% decline in the previous session, Sandisk shares lost another 15% at their intraday low. SK Hynix's ADRs also fell 14% after shares of the South Korean memory maker tumbled in overseas trading, alongside Samsung Electronics. Nvidia shares extended their decline to 9%, marking their biggest drop since April 2025. Similarly, Intel shares declined 10%, while AMD plunged 17%. The AI-led rally has powered Wall Street to multiple record highs this year, even as concerns over inflation, economic policies and the possibility of higher interest rates have weighed on the broader market. Meanwhile, Elon Musk-led Tesla and SpaceX shares extended their declines, falling 9% and 11%, respectively, amid reports that the billionaire had spent at least $445 million to help Republicans retain control of Congress. The steep sell-off also weighed on the broader market, with the S&P 500 falling 4% and the Nasdaq 100 declining as much as 6.4%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index, which tracks US-listed semiconductor stocks, dropped 11%, extending its losses from Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also declined 3%. The artificial intelligence industry has remained volatile for months amid growing criticism that valuations have climbed too high and that the sector could be heading towards a bubble. Investors are also questioning whether the hundreds of billions of dollars that major technology companies are pouring into AI data centres will generate sufficient productivity gains and profits to justify the massive investments. Democrats secured major electoral gains in the midterm elections, including victories in key gubernatorial races. The results could accelerate the backlash against power-hungry, water-intensive and noisy data centres that are central to the AI boom but have become increasingly unpopular among local communities. US President Donald Trump acknowledged that the Iran war had affected the midterm results, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gasoline prices resulting from the more than eight-month-old conflict. Trump has been a strong supporter of the AI industry, and greater Democratic influence in Congress could pave the way for tighter regulation or restrictions on the sector. However, concerns about AI infrastructure and its impact on local communities have been growing across political parties. State-level policy changes could have a more immediate impact on the industry. Democrats won gubernatorial races in Ohio, Georgia and Texas, three states with significant planned data centre investments. These electoral gains could increase regulatory scrutiny of new data centre projects and create additional hurdles for companies looking to expand their AI infrastructure.
